question.text: Ashwath Venture Credit AIF is structuring a venture-debt facility for a Series C SaaS company, Priya Tech Pvt Ltd. The term sheet includes a 2.5-year tenor, senior-secured-with-founder-shares collateral, and an equity kicker via warrants. Industry benchmarks in the chapter suggest venture-debt structures can potentially yield IRRs in the range of:

answer.text: 8-12% p.a., similar to bank MCLR plus 200 bps
25-30% p.a., reflecting the higher risk and warrant conversion upside
12-18% p.a., similar to private credit for established companies
40-50% p.a., on par with pure VC equity IRRs

explanation.text: The Logic: Per Ch 11.1.2 (Venture Debt), the chapter notes venture-debt structures can potentially yield IRRs of over 25-30% to lending funds, though 2024-25 saw moderation as more funds entered. The yield reflects insufficient cash-flow risk at the debtor stage plus warrant upside. The Trap: 8-12% is bank senior debt territory. 12-18% is private credit for established (non-VC-stage) companies. 40-50% is equity VC IRR on winners, not debt IRR. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-A tests venture debt as a Cat II product. XIX-C tests the Manager's pricing lens — IRR must include the equity kicker's expected value, not just the coupon. Manager's Pro-Tip: When pitching venture debt to your IC, decompose the 25-30% target IRR: coupon + warrant MOIC at assumed valuation uplift. If the warrant upside is doing 60%+ of the work, call it quasi-equity and price the risk accordingly.
